title: Discussion on multi-GPU support for cuFFT and cuSOLVER
body_excerpt: Original context: See #2644.  Some of CUDA libraries like cuFFT and cuSOLVER provide native multi-GPU support. However, there is no guarantee that multiple GPUs will outperform single GPU; on the contrary, for cuFFT I found in https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/2644#issuecomment-558835428 that any workload that can be handled in one GPU should ***not*** be processed using multi GPUs; the extra data transfer just kills the performance (even if NVLinks are present). I suspect the same holds for cuSOLVER.  Since CuPy operations incurs additional memory overhead, I think it is clear that multi-GPU is useful only when the workload is too large to fit in one GPU. title: Create a numpy_cupy_allclose with `NULP` (or similar) mechanism
body_excerpt: While the current ability to pass a dict of dtypes to `rtol=` and `atol=` is nice, in practice it is used pretty rarely meaning that double precision routines are often tested with the same precision as single precision ones.  This is mostly fine, since correctness errors should still fail, but it gives very little with respect to testing expected higher precision of `double` versions.  I think it would be helpful to add a testing mechanism based on `assert_array_almost_equal_nulp`.  Or something similar to it, maybe an integer meaning a multiple of the `finfo(...).eps` or so.

body_excerpt: ### Description  `jax.scipy.special.ndtri` returns positive infinity when the argument exceeds `1.0` and negative infinity when the argument is less than `0.0`.  ```python3 from jax import numpy as jnp from jax.scipy.special import ndtri ndtri(jnp.asarray(-1.))  # Array(-inf, dtype=float32) ndtri(jnp.asarray(2.))  # Array(inf, dtype=float32) ```  It seems that it would be more appropriate to return NaN in these cases (as `scipy.special.ndtri`, `torch.special.ndtri`, etc. do).   This came up when adding support for JAX as an array API backend in SciPy. title: Support numpy.isnan and numpy.isnat in cuda.jit kernels
body_excerpt: Currently math.isnan is supported for checking for `NaN`s, but there's no way to check for `NaT`s easily short of viewing as an int64 and comparing to the minimum value (-9223372036854775808). Simple reproducer: ```python import numpy as np from numba import cuda  test_in = cuda.to_device(np.array([1,None,3], dtype='datetime64[ms]')) test_out = cuda.to_device(np.array([1,2,3]))  @cuda.jit def test_datetime_nat(in_array, out_array):     i = cuda.grid(1)     if i < in_array.size:         if np.isnat(in_array[i]):             out_array[i] = 100  test_datetime_nat.forall(test_in.size)(test_in, test_out) ```

title: RFC: Separate NumPy and CPython implementions/functionality.
body_excerpt: This is an RFC on altering Numba's fundamental numerical functionality to better reflect what is present in Python/NumPy. The intended impact of this is to:  * Ensure better reproducibility, i.e. Numba will more closely follow what would happen in the interpreter. * Alter performance characteristics with an anticipated net performance gain. * Create conceptually easier paths to follow to achieve higher performance.  **Current state:**  At present, the Numba code base implements a large number of the functions found in Python builtins, Python's `operator`, `math` and `cmath` modules, and NumPy. title: Runtime integer calculation overflow
body_excerpt: Not sure if this can be classified as a bug but I thought I would post this just incase it isn't known about. Values known at compile time, and are thus computed in Python, use Python's long int and can represent values outside the range of a normal integer so you can get results that don't quite match.  ``` from numba import cuda import numpy as np  @cuda.jit def test_kernel(a,b,c,test): 	i = cuda.grid(1)  	test[0] = a**b%c 	test[1] = 11**19%1009  a, b, c = 11, 19, 1009 test = cuda.device_array(2, dtype = np.uint32)  test_kernel[1, 1](a,b,c,test)  print(a**b%c,test.copy_to_host()) >>> 902 [759 902] ```

title: cuda.grid(1) returns incorrect value due to signed integer overflow
body_excerpt: `cuda.grid(1)` returns an incorrect value in the following code:  ```py import numpy as np from numba import cuda   @cuda.jit def bug(out):     i = cuda.threadIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x     i2 = cuda.grid(1)     if i != i2:         # this shouldn't happen         print(i, i2)   free_mem, _ = cuda.current_context().get_memory_info() # max_num_parallel_iter is around 566281830 on my 4090 max_num_parallel_iter = free_mem // 4 - 128 * 1024 * 1024 dev_out = cuda.device_array(max_num_parallel_iter, dtype=np.float32) bug[22121216, 256](dev_out) ```  One example of a case which is printed is when `i = 2147551327` and `i2 = -214741596`, which likely indicates a signed 32 bit integer overflow. The bug doesn't appear when setting `max_num_parallel_iter` to an int

title: sum and np.sum() algorithm needs to catch up to improved upstream precision
body_excerpt: This is a "narrative" type of bug report, aka "search the code and compare". No test cases are provided here.  Python and NumPy has each changed their `sum()` implementations beyond ordinary linear summation. title: torch.compile: autograd.Function.apply with aliased inputs drops per-slot gradient contributions

body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug  When the same Tensor is passed to two (or more) positional tensor arguments of a `torch.autograd.Function.apply(...)`, and the backward returns different values for those positions (e.g. `None` for one slot and a tensor for another), `torch.compile` produces a graph that drops one of the per-slot gradient contributions.  In eager, autograd accumulates both slot contributions into a single `.grad` on the shared input. title: Remove `volatile` usage in `rolling_detail.cuh` where not required
body_excerpt: In the device code in `rolling_detail.cuh`, there are variables declared as `volatile` to work around compiler optimizations in CUDA 10.x. E.g.: ```c++     // declare this as volatile to avoid some compiler optimizations that lead to incorrect results     // for CUDA 10.0 and below (fixed in CUDA 10.1)     volatile cudf::size_type count = 0; ``` Given that CUDF 0.20 supports CUDA 11.0+, it should now be safe to remove this comment, and the `volatile` attributes.  If not handled in #8158, this can be addressed after #8158 is merged.

title: [FEA] libcudf implementation of "intuitive" decimal division
body_excerpt: The `libcudf` implementation of decimal division is really fixed-point division, and does not behave intuitively compared with the accepted conventions in (say) the SQL world.  For example, dividing `DECIMAL64(200,-2)` by `DECIMAL64(300,-2)` (which is equivalent to `2.00 / 3.00`) gives a result of `DECIMAL64(0,0)` due to the implementation of `fixed_point<>::operator/()` which simply divides the internal integer values and sets the output scale to the input scale difference.  This is not useful in a an SQL context, where the intuitive result would be something like `DECIMAL64(66,-2)` (i.e. `0.66`). title: When upcasting bf16 to fp32 inside the kernel, triton uses TF32 path despite I pass input_precision="ieee"

If I have `x.dtype=torch.bfloat16` and `y.dtype=torch.float32` and do `tl.dot(x.to(y.dtype), y, input_precision="ieee", out_dtype=tl.float32)`, looks like triton will fallback to TF32 precision. However, since I explicitly upcast x to fp32 before I do the matmul and I specified ieee precision, I was expecting triton to take the ieee path instead.  I thought this should yield the same result as upcasting x in pytorch and pass this fp32 x to triton?
